docs.title: Circle Care Product Wiki
docs.text:
Care, in one circle. Circle Care is a privacy-first care-coordination app for an older adult who lives at home, the professional and family caregivers who help them, and the legal guardian who makes decisions with them. It puts everyone on the same daily plan — medicines, tasks, visits, check-ins and emergencies — while the older adult stays in charge of who can see what. This wiki documents the product end to end: why it exists, who it serves, every feature in the working prototype, how it is built and secured, and what comes next.

Concept product — fictional people and data

Circle Care is a portfolio and training product created by Sumanth (Product Owner, Certified Scrum Product Owner) from a CSPO course assignment. Every person, phone number, address, medicine and health reading in the prototype and in this wiki is fictional. No real health information is collected, stored or sent anywhere.

docs.title: Circle Care in 30 seconds
docs.text: What One app with three experiences — elder, caregiver and legal guardian — plus a marketing website. Installable on a phone as a Progressive Web App (PWA). Who Margaret "Maggie" Lee (80, lives alone in San Francisco), her daughter and healthcare power of attorney Sarah, her home care aide Ana, her grandson James, and a time-limited respite caregiver, Ruth. Problem Care for an older adult at home is split across texts, paper notes, phone calls and memory. Doses get missed or doubled, nobody knows who is covering tonight, and the older adult loses privacy and control. Answer A shared daily plan, gentle reminders, verified caregiver check-ins, a self-drafting shift hand-off, a hold-to-send SOS that escalates until someone answers, and a Privacy Center where the elder sees and controls access. Principles Privacy-first · Elder in control · Minimum necessary access. Status Working prototype v0.4. Runs entirely in the browser with encrypted demo data. No backend, no real notifications, not for real patients. North Star Verified care tasks completed on time per week — shown on the guardian's home screen and weekly digest. The public website introduces the product and links into the demo app.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Most older adults want to keep living in their own home. Doing that safely usually depends on a small, informal team: an adult child who handles medical and legal decisions, a paid home care aide for a few hours a day, and other relatives who help on weekends. That team rarely shares one source of truth.

  • Medicines are the highest-risk part of the day. A missed blood-pressure tablet or a double dose of a diabetes medicine is easy when three people are involved and nobody can see what the others did.
  • Coverage is fragile. A late or absent caregiver is often discovered hours later. Uncovered evening shifts go unnoticed until they arrive.
  • Emergencies depend on one phone call being answered. If the first person doesn't pick up, there is no automatic next step.
  • Privacy and dignity are an afterthought. Existing tools tend to treat the older adult as a patient being monitored, not as the person whose information it is.
  • Decision-makers are remote. A legal guardian who lives two hours away learns about problems days later, from someone else.

Circle Care's research plan (see Research & Compliance) frames these as hypotheses to validate with interviews; the prototype exists to make those conversations concrete.

docs.title: Who it serves and what each person gets
docs.text:
Elder (Maggie)Caregiver (Ana)Legal guardian (Sarah)

Value: independence with a safety net.

  • A home screen with exactly three large actions: What's next, SOS, Call my person.
  • Spoken reminders, three text sizes, high contrast and 48 px+ touch targets.
  • A one-tap daily "I'm OK" check-in instead of a worried phone call.
  • A Privacy Center to see who has access, who looked at her information, pause sharing and remove people.
  • Sees every decision made about her care and can ask a question.

Value: know exactly what this shift needs.

  • Check in at the door; today's medicines and tasks unlock only for the shift.
  • Doses in time order with Due now / Late / Overdue states and high-priority medicines called out.
  • Reads the previous caregiver's hand-off before starting.
  • At check-out the hand-off note is drafted automatically from what was logged.
  • Two-week schedule, shift offers and swap requests.

Value: peace of mind from a distance, without micromanaging.

  • Today at a glance: check-in, doses, tasks, who is with Maggie now, health and next appointment.
  • A short Needs your attention list instead of a stream of notifications.
  • Approvals for medicine changes, new members and shift swaps — Maggie sees every decision.
  • Health readings (only while Maggie shares them), a medication-appointment calendar and a weekly digest.
  • Care circle management, SOS order, alert timing and quiet hours.

docs.title: Product principles
docs.text:
1. Privacy-first

Health information stays inside the app. Lock-screen notifications and emails never name a medicine, condition or note. Data is encrypted on the device, every access is logged in a tamper-evident chain, and exports are passphrase-protected.

2. The elder is in control

The circle is built around one person. Maggie confirms members, sees who looked at her information, can pause sharing with one switch (SOS still works), decides whether her health readings are shared, and is told about every decision made about her. Refusing a medicine is recorded as her choice, not as an error.

3. Minimum necessary

Each role sees only what it needs. Professional caregivers see medicines and tasks only while checked in to a shift. Notes can be shared with everyone or with the guardian only. Guardian powers depend on verified legal documents. One permission matrix (src/data/policy.ts) decides every read and write.

docs.title: Regulatory Applicability Memo
docs.text: Notion story: CC-8 Regulatory applicability memo Status: DRAFT for counsel review — not legal advice. Written by the product owner from general knowledge as of 2026-10-19. No lawyer has reviewed it. Every conclusion below is a working assumption to be confirmed or corrected by qualified counsel before launch or pilot.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: Identify which laws likely apply to Circle Care, under which business models, so the backlog includes the right controls and counsel's time is focused on the right questions.

docs.title: 2. Product facts relevant to the analysis
docs.text:
• Circle Care stores, for one older adult ("the elder"): medication list and schedule, dose logs (taken/skipped/refused), care tasks, visit check-ins, care notes, uploaded documents (care plans, discharge summaries, legal authority documents), an emergency card (allergies, conditions, directives, blood type), SOS events, daily check-ins, and an access log. See CC-9 data inventory.
  • Users: the elder, a verified legal guardian/healthcare POA, family members, professional caregivers (agency-employed or private), and an internal review team that verifies legal documents.
  • Channels: in-app, push, SMS, email. Lock-screen and email text is designed to carry no health information (CC-31; Digest email "carries no PHI").
  • Current prototype is browser-only with fictional data; nothing is transmitted. This memo is about the production product.

docs.title: 3.1 When HIPAA likely does not apply directly
docs.text: HIPAA applies to covered entities (health plans, clearinghouses, providers who conduct standard electronic transactions) and their business associates. When a family downloads Circle Care and uses it on its own, Circle Care is likely a consumer health app, not a covered entity or business associate, even though it holds health information.

docs.title: 3.2 When Circle Care likely is a business associate
docs.text: Scenario Likely status (to confirm) A home-care agency that is a HIPAA covered entity contracts with Circle Care to coordinate its clients' care Circle Care = business associate of the agency; BAA required A health system or Medicaid waiver program offers Circle Care to patients and receives data back Likely business associate A private-pay caregiver (not a covered entity) uses Circle Care HIPAA likely does not apply via that caregiver An agency that does not bill electronically (may not be a covered entity) Unclear — counsel question Q2 Mixed: one circle includes an agency caregiver (BA relationship) and family (consumer) Unclear which data is PHI under the BAA — Q3

docs.title: 3.3 Plan: operate as HIPAA-ready regardless
docs.text:
Because the business model may include agencies, and because the same data is equally sensitive either way, Circle Care plans to meet the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules as a design standard for all circles:

  • Security Rule safeguards: risk analysis (CC-79), access control (CC-18/19), audit controls (CC-28), integrity, transmission security, workforce training, contingency planning.
  • Minimum necessary: caregivers see the plan only on shift (pro@shift).
  • Individual rights mirrored as product features: access/export (CC-32), access log (CC-29), amendment (open: no "request a correction" flow yet).
  • BAAs with every vendor that may touch health data (CC-30).
  • Breach response (CC-34).

The public Privacy page already states this posture ("designed to the HIPAA standard… even where HIPAA doesn't legally apply"). Counsel must review that wording before it is used publicly (Q1).

docs.title: 4. FTC Act §5 and the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (HBNR)
docs.text:
• Section 5 (unfair or deceptive practices): every privacy promise on the website and in the app is a representation the FTC can enforce. The "Things we will never do" list on /privacy must be true in production (e.g., "Use analytics that can identify a person"). Track each promise as a testable requirement.
  • HBNR (16 CFR Part 318): applies to vendors of personal health records and related entities not covered by HIPAA. As amended (2024), it is understood to cover health apps that draw information from multiple sources; Circle Care draws from the elder, caregivers and family, and possibly device/health integrations later. A "breach" includes unauthorized disclosures, not only hacks — e.g., sharing with an analytics vendor without authorization.
  • Implication: in consumer mode, a breach could require notice to individuals, the FTC and possibly media. Timelines differ from HIPAA. Counsel to confirm (Q4).

Visit check-in uses location — confirm how (Q6). Similar state health-data laws (e.g., Nevada, Connecticut amendments) Similar consumer health data concepts Maintain a state-law tracker California CMIA May apply to businesses offering software designed to maintain medical information for consumers Confidentiality obligations; restrictions on disclosure California CCPA/CPRA Applies if thresholds are met; "sensitive personal information" includes health Notice at collection, right to limit use of sensitive PI, deletion, access State breach notification laws All states; many include medical information Track state-by-state timelines in CC-34 State guardianship/POA statutes Validity and scope of authority vary by state See §8 State EVV rules (Medicaid personal care) If agencies use Circle Care for Medicaid visits Circle Care is not an EVV system; don't market as one

docs.title: 6. TCPA (SMS and calls)
docs.text:
• SMS reminders and alerts to circle members are likely informational, but TCPA consent rules still apply for automated texts to mobile numbers.
  • Plan: obtain express consent per phone number at invite acceptance (CC-17), honor STOP/HELP, record consent with timestamp, respect quiet hours (default 22:00–07:00 in settings.quietHours; SOS bypass is a design choice to review — criticalBypass).
  • Elder's number may be entered by a guardian: confirm who can consent on the elder's behalf (Q8).
  • SMS carries no PHI by design. SOS SMS fallback (via: "sms-fallback") must also be PHI-free.
  • Carrier registration (10DLC) and provider terms — operational, not legal, but blocks launch.

docs.title: 7. Accessibility — ADA and WCAG
docs.text:
• The prototype aims for WCAG 2.2 AA (README). Title III's application to apps and websites is subject to evolving case law and DOJ guidance; if Circle Care contracts with state Medicaid programs or public entities, Title II web rules with WCAG 2.1 AA may apply via contract.
  • Plan: WCAG 2.2 AA as the bar; automated (axe-core) plus manual screen reader testing (VoiceOver, TalkBack) and testing with older adults. See CC-78.

docs.title: 8. Guardianship / POA document handling
docs.text:
• Documents uploaded as "Legal authority" are reviewed by the internal review team (/app/review, CC-24). Reviewers see only the legal document queue.
  • Questions: what does a reviewer actually need to confirm (name match, signature, court seal, activation/springing conditions, expiration, scope — healthcare vs. financial)? What liability arises if a reviewer approves a forged or revoked document?
  • Retention: legal documents are highly sensitive; keep only as long as needed to evidence the verification decision (Q10).
  • Scope limits: a healthcare POA may not authorize everything in the app (e.g., removing family members). Map app permissions to typical authority scope.
  • Product tension to flag: the elder retains rights even with a guardian. Today the policy lets the guardian approve med changes and write settings; the elder is notified of every decision (CC-65) but cannot block them.

docs.title: 9. Other areas to check
docs.text:
• FDA: Circle Care does not diagnose or recommend treatment; medication reminders and adherence logging are generally viewed as low-risk wellness/administrative functions. Confirm no feature crosses into device software (e.g., dose recommendations).
  • Elder abuse mandatory reporting: if the review team or support staff see evidence of abuse, are there reporting obligations? (Q12)
  • COPPA: not expected (no users under 13), but family members could include minors (e.g., grandchildren). Set a minimum age.
  • Electronic signatures / consent records: consent version and timestamp are stored (settings.consent, CC-22), including "on behalf" consent with a documented reason.

docs.title: 10. Open questions for counsel
docs.text: # Question Q1 Is the public statement "designed to the HIPAA standard… even where HIPAA doesn't legally apply" acceptable, or does it create misleading expectations? Q2 Which home-care agencies are covered entities (e.g., private-pay-only agencies)? How should contracts differ? Q3 In a mixed circle, which data is PHI under a BAA and which is consumer data? Can one data store serve both? Q4 Does the amended HBNR apply in consumer mode? What counts as a "breach of security" for us? Q5 What do we need to meet the MHMDA (policy, consent flows, deletion timelines)? Does it apply if we have no WA users at launch? Q6 Does door check-in location capture create "precise location" or geofencing issues under state laws? Q7 Do CMIA and CCPA/CPRA apply at our expected size? Q8 Who may consent to SMS on an elder's behalf (guardian, POA)? Q9 Is our SOS feature at risk of being perceived as a monitored emergency service? What disclaimers are needed? Q10 Minimum and maximum retention for legal authority documents and audit logs (currently 6 years — RETENTION_YEARS). Q11 Liability allocation if guardian verification is wrong; insurance needs. Q12 Any reporting obligations when staff see signs of elder abuse or neglect? Q13 Elder's right of access: guardian-only notes (notes.private) are hidden from the elder by policy. Is that permissible where HIPAA applies?

docs.title: Retention and deletion (intended)
docs.text:
• Close the circle (elder or guardian, data.delete): prototype wipes circle state, destroys the device key and clears the file store (wipeDevice, CC-33), so any leftover copy is unreadable. Production: delete within 30 days (as promised on /privacy), including backups on their normal rotation.
  • Audit log: kept at least 6 years (RETENTION_YEARS = 6 in src/data/audit.ts) — minimal entries only (IDs, action, resource name). Confirm with counsel (CC-8 Q10).
  • Member removed / time limit ends (CC-25): access stops immediately; their authored records stay with the circle (they are part of the elder's care record).

docs.title: Vendor and BAA Register
docs.text: Notion story: CC-30 Vendor BAA register Status: TEMPLATE — no vendors selected, no contracts or BAAs signed. Every row needs an owner. Not legal advice; BAA requirements to be confirmed by counsel (CC-8).

docs.title: Rules for this register
docs.text:
1. Default to PHI-free. For every vendor, first ask: can we design so this vendor never receives PHI? If yes, document the design control and verify it in testing. If no, a signed BAA is required before any production data flows.
  2. A BAA is necessary but not sufficient: also review the vendor's security posture (SOC 2 Type II / HITRUST report, encryption, breach notice terms, subprocessors, data location, deletion on termination).
  3. Free tiers and consumer plans of most vendors do not include BAAs. Confirm the specific plan.
  4. Even where HIPAA does not apply (consumer mode), keep the same controls; the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule and state laws treat unauthorized sharing as a breach.
  5. Review each row at least yearly and whenever the vendor's use changes.

docs.title: Pilot Plan
docs.text: Notion story: CC-74 Run a pilot with 15–25 care circles Status: DRAFT plan — pilot not started; no circles recruited. Proposed start May 2027 (as stated on the /pilot page). Blocked on production readiness items listed in §9.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
Learn, with real families over 8 weeks, whether Circle Care increases verified care tasks completed on time (North Star, CC-6) without making the elder feel watched, and whether caregivers and guardians would keep using it.

The pilot is a learning exercise, not a launch. We expect to find things that don't work.

docs.title: 2. Pilot size and mix
docs.text:
• 15–25 care circles. Below 15, per-persona NPS cohorts will often fall under the minimum of 5 and be hidden on the dashboard.
  • Target mix:
  • at least 8 circles with a professional caregiver visiting (to test shift mode);
  • at least 5 circles with a long-distance guardian;
  • at least 3 states (state-law differences, CC-8);
  • elders with a range of phone comfort.

docs.title: 3. Eligibility
docs.text: Criterion Rule Elder 65+, lives at home or with family, able to give her own consent to join (no proxy consent for the pilot in v1) Guardian / POA Holds healthcare POA or guardianship; willing to upload documents for review (CC-24) Circle At least 2 members besides the elder Devices Elder has an iPhone or Android phone, or a tablet at home; others have smartphones Medicines Elder takes 2+ scheduled medicines Exclusions Hospice or end-of-life care; elder in a facility; anyone employed by a competing product; circles currently in a crisis (recent hospitalization within 2 weeks) — invite later Agencies If an agency caregiver joins, written agency permission; if the agency is a HIPAA covered entity, a BAA must be in place first (CC-8, CC-30)

docs.title: 4. Recruiting via /pilot
docs.text:
• The /pilot page form asks: name, email or phone, role, state, whether a professional caregiver visits, and consent to be contacted. It warns "Please don't include any health information here."
  • In the prototype, only role, state and hasPro are stored (addPilotLead in src/lib/pilot.ts); name and contact are dropped. Production must store contact details in a separate, access-restricted store so we can call people back — and delete them after the pilot.
  • The page promises "We'll reach out within two weeks." Assign an owner to keep that promise.
  • Additional channels: the CC-1 channels (AAAs, senior centers, agencies, support groups); interview participants who opted in.
  • Screening call (15 min) using a short version of the CC-1 screener.

docs.title: 5. Onboarding — white-glove setup call (CC-75)
docs.text:
30-minute call per circle, elder present.

  1. Introductions; explain what the pilot is and isn't (not an emergency monitoring service).
  2. Consent: walk through plain-language consent with read-aloud (CC-22); elder consents herself.
  3. Create the circle; invite members by role; set time-bound access for respite caregivers (CC-25).
  4. Guardian uploads legal document; explain review time.
  5. Enter medicines with the guardian; mark high-priority medicines.
  6. Set check-in window, escalation order, quiet hours.
  7. Elder: choose text size and contrast; try What's next, SOS hold-and-cancel, Call my person.
  8. Show the Privacy Center: who can see, access log, Pause sharing.
  9. Agree on support contact and what to do in a real emergency (call 911 first).

In-app: first-run tour per persona and a "request a setup call" option (settings.setupCallRequested, CC-75).

docs.title: 6. Timeline (8 weeks)
docs.text:
Week Activity −4 to −1 Recruit, screen, schedule setup calls; production readiness gate (§9) 0 Setup calls; baseline survey (how many check-in calls per day today, time spent coordinating) 1 Day-3 check-in call (short); fix onboarding issues 2–3 Normal use; monitor dashboard weekly 4 Mid-point check-in (15 min per persona); in-app NPS prompt 5–7 Normal use; targeted interviews on emerging themes 8 Final conversation (30 min); final NPS; exit survey +2 Synthesis; go/no-go recommendation

Matches the /pilot page promise: "A 30-minute setup call, two short check-ins, and a final conversation."

docs.title: 7. Success metrics
docs.text:
Viewed on the internal pilot dashboard /app/pilot (CC-77). The prototype dashboard currently shows a "Sample cohort" of invented numbers to design the layout — not results.

Metric Definition Target Source North Star Verified care tasks completed on time per circle per week (median) Rising week over week; baseline set in weeks 1–2 Dose and task logs Dose confirmation rate Scheduled doses with a taken/skipped/refused record ÷ scheduled doses ≥90% (dashboard goal) doses Daily check-in rate Days with an "I'm OK" in the window ÷ pilot days ≥80% by week 8 checkins Alert answered time Median minutes from critical/warning alert to acknowledgment <10 min median Alerts, SOS acknowledgments NPS by persona % 9–10 minus % 0–6, per elder / caregiver / guardian Report only where n ≥ 5 (MIN_COHORT); targets set after baseline In-app feedback (CC-76) Weekly active circles Circles with any activity in the week ≥80% of enrolled through week 8 Aggregates Guardrails Sharing paused 7+ days; members removed; alert volume per guardian per week Watch and follow up, no target Aggregates

Qualitative: did the elder feel more or less in control? Did caregivers save time? Did guardians call less?

docs.title: 8. Consent and data handling
docs.text:
• Pilot data is separate from circle data (src/lib/pilot.ts pattern): pilot leads and NPS responses live in their own store with no link to circle records.
  • De-identified: dashboard shows aggregates only; groups under 5 hidden; free-text feedback scrubbed of health terms (scrubHealth) and never shown on the dashboard.
  • Deletion: pilot research data is deleted 12 months after the pilot ends (stated on the dashboard). Circle data follows normal product rules: a family that leaves can close the circle and have data deleted (the /pilot page says "Your data is deleted when you do").
  • Interview notes follow CC-1 de-identification rules.
  • No data used for anything other than improving Circle Care; no sale, no advertising.
  • Incentive: free for life for pilot families plus a thank-you gift card (as promised on /pilot) — budget and legal review of "free for life" needed.

docs.title: 9. Production readiness gate (must be true before week 0)
docs.text:
• [ ] Real backend with server-side permission checks (CC-19) — currently none.
  • [ ] Real push/SMS delivery with PHI-free content and tested SOS fallback.
  • [ ] BAAs in place for vendors that may touch PHI (CC-30).
  • [ ] HIPAA security risk analysis reviewed (CC-79).
  • [ ] Incident response roles assigned; tabletop run (CC-34).
  • [ ] External pen test completed and highs fixed (CC-78).
  • [ ] Counsel reviewed consent text, privacy policy, pilot terms (CC-8).

docs.title: 10. Exit criteria
docs.text:
Continue to broader beta if all are true: - Dose confirmation ≥90% in weeks 5–8 for most circles. - Median alert answered under 10 minutes. - At least 70% of circles still active in week 8. - No SEV-1 incidents; any SEV-2 resolved with root cause fixed. - Elders, in final conversations, mostly report feeling in control (qualitative).

Stop or rethink if any is true: - A safety failure (SOS or escalation not delivered) that we can't explain and fix. - Elders report feeling surveilled in a majority of circles. - Caregivers report net added time in a majority of circles.

Participant exit at any time: circle closed and data deleted on request; NPS responses already given stay de-identified in the research store until its deletion date — disclose this in consent.

docs.title: 11. Human actions
docs.text:
• [ ] Assign pilot owner and support contact.
  • [ ] Production readiness gate (§9).
  • [ ] Budget for incentives and setup-call time.
  • [ ] Counsel review of consent and "free for life" promise.

docs.text:
Notion story: CC-1 Recruit and screen interview participants Status: DRAFT / TEMPLATE. No participants have been recruited or contacted. Every step below needs a human to run it.

Circle Care is a CSPO-training concept product. This plan describes how discovery interviews would be run. Nothing here reports real research.

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
Recruit enough people across the three personas to test whether the core problems Circle Care is built around are real, frequent and painful:

  • Elders (like Margaret "Maggie" Lee): staying independent while accepting help, and keeping control over who knows what.
  • Professional caregivers (like Ana Rivera): proving work was done, and hand-offs between shifts.
  • Legal guardians / healthcare POA holders (like Sarah Lee): knowing Mom is OK without calling five times a day, and making decisions with good information.

Secondary: family helpers (like grandson James) and respite caregivers (like Ruth Okafor). Interview 1–2 of each if they come up naturally, but they do not count toward quotas.

Where possible, recruit linked triads (an elder, their caregiver and their guardian) — at least 2 triads — so we can compare how each person describes the same situation. Interview each person separately.

docs.title: 5. Consent form outline (needs review before use)
docs.text:
Plain language, 14pt+ print, read aloud for elders. Draft sections:

  1. Who we are and that Circle Care is a student/concept project, not a company selling anything.
  2. What we will ask about (daily routines, help, privacy) and how long it takes.
  3. Taking part is voluntary; you can skip any question or stop at any time and still receive the incentive.
  4. Recording: audio only, with separate opt-in; notes taken either way.
  5. Please do not tell us specific diagnoses, medicine names or doctors' names. If you do, we will remove them from notes.
  6. How data is stored, who sees it (only the research team), and when it is deleted (recordings within 30 days of transcription; de-identified notes within 12 months).
  7. Quotes may be used without names or identifying details.
  8. Contact for questions or withdrawal.
  9. Signature or recorded verbal consent with date.

Human action: have the consent text reviewed (e.g., by an instructor or IRB-style reviewer) before first use. Elders who cannot consent for themselves are excluded; we do not take proxy consent for research.

  • In notes: replace names with role words ("my daughter", "the aide"); replace medicine names with "[med]"; replace conditions with "[condition]"; replace employer/agency names with "[agency]"; generalize location to state.
  • Never paste notes into tools that train on inputs.
  • Recordings: store encrypted, delete within 30 days after transcription.

docs.title: Interview Guide — Elders
docs.text:
Notion story: CC-2 Interview guide: elders Status: DRAFT. Not yet piloted or used. No interviews have taken place.

Participants come through the CC-1 screener. Only interview people who can give their own consent. Session length 45–60 minutes. Offer breaks.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Understand a typical day: what help arrives, from whom, and how the person feels about it.
  2. Learn how medicines are managed today and where it goes wrong.
  3. Understand what independence, dignity and control mean to this person in concrete terms — what they would and would not want others to know.
  4. Learn what they do when something goes wrong (a fall, feeling unwell, a missed visit).
  5. React to three prototype tasks: the three-button home, confirming a dose, and the Privacy Center.

docs.title: Interviewer reminders
docs.text:
• Sit at eye level, face the person, speak clearly but do not talk down. Use their preferred name.
  • Ask about past behavior, not hypotheticals ("Tell me about the last time…").
  • Do not correct or teach. If they struggle with the prototype, that is data.
  • If they mention a diagnosis or medicine name, do not write it down; note "[condition]" / "[med]".
  • If they disclose risk of harm (neglect, abuse, an unsafe situation), pause the interview and follow the safety protocol agreed with the research lead before fieldwork starts (human action: write this protocol).

docs.title: 1. Warm-up (5 min)
docs.text:
• Thank you for having me. How long have you lived here?
  • What does a good day look like for you?
  • Who are the people you see or talk to most in a week?

docs.title: 2. Daily life and help (10 min)
docs.text:
• Walk me through yesterday from when you woke up.
  • Who helps you with anything? What do they help with?
  • How did that help start? Whose idea was it?
  • What do you still do entirely on your own that matters to you?
  • Is there anything people help with that you'd rather do yourself?

docs.title: 3. Medicines (8 min)
docs.text:
• How do you keep track of your medicines today? (pill box, alarm, someone reminds you)
  • Tell me about the last time a dose was missed or taken twice. What happened? Who found out?
  • When someone reminds you about medicine, how does it feel? Does it depend on who reminds you?
  • If you decide to skip a dose on purpose, who should know? Who should not?

docs.title: 4. Independence, dignity and control (12 min) — core
docs.text:
• When your daughter/son or a caregiver checks on you, how does that feel?
  • Has anyone ever known something about you that you wish they hadn't? How did they find out?
  • If you could decide exactly who sees what — medicines, notes from the aide, your appointments — how would you split it?
  • Is there anything you'd want only your [guardian/daughter] to see, and not the aide? Anything the other way around?
  • If you could switch off everyone's view for a while, would you ever use that? When?
  • Has anyone ever made a decision about your care without asking you? Tell me about it.
  • What would make you feel "checked up on" versus "looked after"?

Probe: "You said ___. Can you tell me more about that?" / "What made that feel that way?"

docs.title: 5. When something goes wrong (7 min)
docs.text:
• Tell me about the last time you needed help quickly. What did you do?
  • Do you have a button, pendant or phone setting for emergencies? Do you wear/use it? Why or why not?
  • Who do you want called first? Does that change at night?
  • How do you feel about a daily "I'm OK" tap each morning? (Ask after exploring how people check on them today.)

docs.title: 6. Concept test — prototype tasks (12 min)
docs.text:
Use the prototype at /#/app → Maggie, on a phone held by the participant. Set text size to their preference first. Read each task aloud; do not demonstrate.

Task Prompt Watch for Success = T1 Three-button home "This is a phone app. What do you think you can do here?" Does the person read all three buttons? Do they fear pressing SOS by accident? Names at least 2 of the 3 actions without help T2 Confirm a dose "It's time for your morning tablet. Show me how you'd tell the app you took it." Then: "Now imagine you decided not to take it." Finds "What's next"; finds taken/skipped/refused; reaction to the word "refused"; tries voice? Records "taken" and a non-taken status unaided T3 Privacy Center "You'd like to see who can look at your information." Then: "Now you want a break from sharing." Understands the list of people; reaction to the access log; finds Pause sharing; understands SOS still works Finds the list and pause switch; explains in own words what pause does T4 Hold SOS (optional) "Show me what you'd do if you fell and needed help." Is the 2-second hold discoverable? Is the 10-second cancel reassuring or stressful? Starts SOS and cancels unaided

After each task: "On a scale of 1 to 5, how easy was that?" and "What would you change?"

Close the concept test with: "Who in your life would you want in a circle like this? Who would you leave out?"

docs.title: 7. Wrap-up (3 min)
docs.text:
• Is there anything about getting help at home that I should have asked and didn't?
  • Would you be open to a 15-minute follow-up?
  • Confirm incentive delivery. Thank them.

docs.title: Interview Guide — Professional Caregivers
docs.text:
Notion story: CC-3 Interview guide: professional caregivers Status: DRAFT. Not yet piloted or used. No interviews have taken place.

Participants come through the CC-1 screener. If the caregiver works for an agency and the agency required approval, confirm written approval is on file. Never ask for client names. Session length 45–60 minutes; schedule around shifts and offer evenings.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Understand a real shift end to end: arrival, tasks, medicines, documentation, leaving.
  2. Measure the workload of documentation and communication today (tools, duplicate entry, time spent).
  3. Understand how caregivers prove work was done (verification) and how they feel about being checked.
  4. Understand hand-offs between caregivers and to family/guardians.
  5. React to three prototype tasks: shift check-in, giving a dose, and end-of-shift hand-off.

docs.title: Interviewer reminders
docs.text:
• Caregivers may worry this is an evaluation. Say clearly: "We are not checking your work, and your employer will not see what you say."
  • Ask about the last shift, not shifts in general.
  • No client names, no medicine names, no addresses. Use "[client]", "[med]".
  • Respect language preference; offer an interpreter if needed (budget TBD).

docs.title: 1. Warm-up (5 min)
docs.text:
• How long have you been a caregiver? What got you into it?
  • What kind of clients do you usually work with?
  • What's the best part of the job? The hardest?

docs.title: 2. The last shift (12 min)
docs.text:
• Walk me through your last shift from when you arrived at the door.
  • How did you know what you needed to do that day?
  • What did you write down or record? Where? When — during or after?
  • Did anything not go to plan? What did you do, and who did you tell?
  • How did you leave things for the next person?

docs.title: 3. Workload and tools (10 min) — core
docs.text:
• How many apps, forms or notebooks do you use for one client? Show me if you can (without client details).
  • About how many minutes per shift go to writing things down or texting family?
  • Is any of that unpaid time (before/after the shift)?
  • What do you enter more than once?
  • Which messages from family are useful? Which take time without helping?
  • If you could get rid of one documentation task, what would it be?

Probe on numbers: "Roughly — 5 minutes? 30?" Record their estimate, not ours.

docs.title: 4. Verification and trust (10 min) — core
docs.text:
• How does your agency or the family know you arrived on time? (EVV, GPS app, sign-in sheet, text)
  • How do you feel about location check-in at the door?
  • Has a family ever doubted that something was done? What happened?
  • What would make you feel protected rather than watched?
  • Who should see your notes? Should some notes go only to the guardian?
  • How do you feel about only seeing the client's care plan while you're on shift?

docs.title: 5. Medicines (6 min)
docs.text:
• What exactly do you do with medicines — remind, hand over, open containers, administer?
  • What happens when the client refuses a dose?
  • When a medicine changes, how do you find out? Has that ever gone wrong?

docs.title: 6. Concept test — prototype tasks (12 min)
docs.text:
Use /#/app → Ana on a phone. Read each task aloud.

Task Prompt Watch for Success = T1 Check in "You just arrived at Maggie's. Start your shift." Finds check-in; reaction to plan unlocking only on shift; manual-reason flow Checks in unaided T2 Give a dose "Maggie's morning medicine is due. Record that she took it." Then: "She says no to the evening one." Order of doses; high-priority callout; recording a refusal Records taken + refused T3 Hand-off "Your shift is over. Leave things for the next person." Reads the auto-drafted summary; edits or accepts; trust in the draft Sends hand-off; says whether they'd trust the draft T4 Shift swap (optional) "You can't make Thursday. Ask someone to cover." Expects the guardian to approve? Finds the flow

After each: "1–5, how easy?" and "Would this save you time or add time compared to today?"

docs.title: 7. Wrap-up (3 min)
docs.text:
• What would make you not want to use an app like this?
  • Would your agency allow it? Who decides?
  • Follow-up OK? Confirm incentive.

docs.title: Interview Guide — Legal Guardians and Healthcare POA Holders
docs.text:
Notion story: CC-4 Interview guide: legal guardians Status: DRAFT. Not yet piloted or used. No interviews have taken place.

Participants come through the CC-1 screener. Do not ask to see legal documents. Do not ask for the elder's name or diagnoses. Session 45–60 minutes; many guardians work full time, so offer evenings and weekends.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Understand how the guardian knows, day to day, whether the elder is OK.
  2. Measure the workload: calls, texts, apps, time off work, coordination with caregivers and family.
  3. Understand how they verify that care actually happened (doses, visits) and how much they trust what they hear.
  4. Understand decision-making: what they approve, how they involve the elder, and where they feel the tension between protecting and respecting autonomy.
  5. Learn what proving legal authority has been like (with hospitals, pharmacies, agencies).
  6. React to prototype tasks: today at a glance, approvals, SOS response, and the weekly digest.

docs.title: Interviewer reminders
docs.text:
• Guardians often carry guilt and stress. Be warm; allow pauses. Do not offer advice.
  • Ask about the last week, specific events.
  • If they mention a crisis that is ongoing, check they're OK to continue.

docs.title: 1. Warm-up (5 min)
docs.text:
• Tell me a bit about yourself and the person you care for (relationship, no names).
  • How did you become their POA / guardian?
  • Who else is involved in their care?

docs.title: 2. Knowing they're OK (10 min)
docs.text:
• How did you know yesterday that they were OK? Walk me through it.
  • How many times in a typical day do you call, text or check something?
  • Tell me about the last time you didn't know and worried. What did you do?
  • What are you most afraid of missing?

docs.title: 3. Workload (8 min) — core
docs.text:
• What tools do you use to coordinate? (group texts, calendar, notebook, agency portal, spreadsheet)
  • How much time per week goes to coordinating care? Any time off work?
  • Who do you have to chase for information?
  • What falls through the cracks?

docs.title: 4. Verification and trust (8 min) — core
docs.text:
• How do you know a medicine was actually taken? A visit actually happened?
  • Has there been a time you found out something hadn't been done? How did you find out, and how long later?
  • What proof would be enough without making the caregiver feel watched?
  • How do you want to hear about a missed dose — immediately, after a delay, only if the caregiver doesn't fix it?

docs.title: 5. Decisions and autonomy (10 min) — core
docs.text:
• What kinds of decisions do you make for them? Which do they still make?
  • Tell me about a recent decision. How did you involve them?
  • Has there been a disagreement between what you thought was safe and what they wanted? What happened?
  • If they wanted to stop sharing information with family or the aide for a while, how would you feel? Should that apply to you?
  • Should they be told about every decision you make? Why or why not?

docs.title: 6. Proving authority (4 min)
docs.text:
• When have you had to show your POA or guardianship papers? How did that go?
  • How long would you accept waiting for an app to verify your documents before you get guardian access?

docs.title: 7. Concept test — prototype tasks (12 min)
docs.text:
Use /#/app → Sarah. Use presenter controls to set up scenarios before each task (e.g., Simulate a missed dose).

Time to answer; which signals they trust Answers correctly in under 30 seconds T2 Missed dose (After Simulate a missed dose) "Something needs your attention." Finds the flag; understands escalation order (caregiver first) Identifies the issue and a next action T3 Approval "Ana has asked for a change. Decide." Reads detail; wants to ask Mom first?; notices the elder is notified Approves or declines with a note T4 SOS response (After Maggie presses SOS) "Respond." Finds "I'm on my way"; expectations about calling 911 Acknowledges SOS T5 Weekly digest "Your brother wants a summary of the week." Would they forward it? Is anything missing or too much? Explains what's in it

After each: "1–5, how easy?" and "Would this replace something you do today? What?"

docs.title: 8. Wrap-up (3 min)
docs.text:
• What would stop you from inviting the whole family and the caregiver into an app like this?
  • What would you pay, if anything? Who pays today for care tools?
  • Follow-up OK? Confirm incentive.

docs.title: Synthesis process (after interviews)
docs.text:
Run within 5 working days of the last interview, with at least 2 people.

  1. Prepare. Print or paste each de-identified note into a whiteboard tool. One observation per sticky: a quote, an action, or a pain point. Tag each with participant ID and segment color (elder orange, caregiver teal, guardian indigo — matching the app).
  2. Silent sort (30 min). Each person groups stickies by similarity without talking. No pre-defined categories.
  3. Name clusters (30 min). Discuss and give each cluster a sentence label in the participant's voice ("I don't know what the aide writes about me"), not a feature name.
  4. Count. For each cluster, record how many distinct participants and segments contributed. A cluster needs 3+ participants to be a theme.
  5. Check hypotheses. For each hypothesis (H-E, H-C, H-G), mark supported / mixed / not supported / not tested*, citing participant IDs.
  6. Look for contradictions across triads. Where elder, caregiver and guardian in the same triad describe the same event differently, write it down; these are design tensions (e.g., safety vs. autonomy).
  7. Update the journeys. Replace hypothesis cells with evidence; strike through cells that were wrong. Change the status line to "Evidence-based, v1 (date)".
  8. Feed CC-6. Move the top themes into the opportunity solution tree as opportunities; retire opportunities with no evidence.

docs.title: Desired outcome (North Star)
docs.text:
Verified care tasks completed on time, per circle, per week.

  • Care task = a scheduled dose or a scheduled care task (meal, shower, walk…).
  • Verified = confirmed in the app by the elder or a circle member, with a caregiver-verified flag where the dose was given during a visit (DoseLog.verified, CC-41).
  • On time = confirmed within the escalation window (dose: before the caregiver escalation at 30 min, settings.doseEscalation.caregiverMin).
  • Measured per circle, per week; reported as the median across circles on the pilot dashboard (CC-77).

Why this metric: it rises only when the elder is safer and the circle has less doubt. It does not reward sending more notifications or collecting more data.

Guardrail metrics (must not get worse): - Elder-initiated privacy actions that indicate distress (members removed, sharing paused for 7+ days) — watch, don't suppress. - Alert volume per guardian per week (alert fatigue). - Refused doses must be recorded honestly; a "refused" is not a failure of the metric — it counts as a verified task outcome.

docs.title: 4. Positioning gaps Circle Care targets (hypotheses)
docs.text:
1. Nobody puts the elder in charge of the circle. Family tools (CaringBridge, Lotsa, Life360) are built for the family; agency tools are built for the agency. Circle Care's bet: the elder owns the circle, sees an access log and can pause sharing. Validate with H-E2, H-E3.
  2. Family tools and agency tools don't meet. Agency software verifies visits but families rarely see it in real time; family tools have no idea a paid caregiver exists. Circle Care's shift mode (pro@shift) bridges this. Validate with H-C6 and T8 in CC-6.
  3. Medication apps stop at the individual. Single-user med apps remind but escalate weakly, and don't distinguish a refusal from a miss. Circle Care records taken/skipped/refused and escalates caregiver-first. Validate with H-E4, H-G3.
  4. Medical alert is a device business. Pendant services offer professional monitoring Circle Care does not. Circle Care should not claim to replace a monitored alert service. Position SOS as "alert your circle," and consider partnering rather than competing.
  5. Legal authority is unverified everywhere. Most family apps let anyone call themselves "guardian." Verified guardian status (CC-24) is a trust differentiator — and an operational cost.

docs.title: 4. Prototype vs. production summary
docs.text:
Demonstrated (browser, fictional data): permission matrix and pro@shift; sharing pause; hash-chained audit; device encryption; encrypted file store with signature checks; passphrase export; PHI-free alert titles; session lock; lockout notice; Sign out everywhere (state only); suspicious access rules; guardian document review queue; CSP on build.

docs.title: Incident Response Runbook
docs.text: Notion story: CC-34 Incident response runbook Status: DRAFT — not adopted, roles not assigned, tabletop exercise not yet run. Notification timelines must be confirmed with counsel; this is not legal advice.

docs.title: 1. What counts as an incident
docs.text: Any event that may have exposed, altered, or made unavailable circle data, or that stops safety features (SOS, escalation, dose reminders) from working. When unsure, open an incident — closing one is cheap.

docs.title: 2. Severity levels
docs.text: Sev Definition Examples Response start Updates SEV-1 Confirmed or likely PHI exposure across circles, or safety features down for many circles Database exposed; SOS delivery failing platform-wide; leaked export from many accounts Immediately, 24/7 Every 30 min internally SEV-2 PHI exposure limited to one circle, or a safety feature degraded Lost caregiver phone with an unlocked session; suspicious access confirmed; SMS provider outage with push working Within 1 hour Every 2 hours SEV-3 Security weakness without known exposure Vulnerability report; misconfigured log found with no PHI Within 1 business day Daily SEV-4 Questions, false alarms Suspicious-access alert that the guardian confirms was expected Within 2 business days On close

docs.title: 3. Roles (names TBD)

docs.title: 4. First-hour checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Open an incident channel and doc; record start time (UTC) and who reported it.
  • [ ] Assign IC and scribe.
  • [ ] Set initial severity (can change).
  • [ ] Safety first: are SOS and escalation still working? If not, tell affected guardians by another channel to check on the elder directly.
  • [ ] Preserve evidence: snapshot logs, do not delete or rotate anything yet unless containment requires it; export audit chain and run verifyChain equivalent.
  • [ ] Contain (see scenarios).
  • [ ] Identify affected circles, data elements (use CC-9), and time window.
  • [ ] Notify privacy officer; if PHI may be involved, start the breach assessment clock (discovery date matters).
  • [ ] Decide next update time.

docs.title: 5.1 Lost or stolen caregiver phone
docs.text:
1. Caregiver or guardian reports it (in-app or support).
  2. Guardian (or support, verified) uses Sign out everywhere for that member (CC-27). In the prototype this signs out all personas and alerts the guardian; in production it must revoke every server session and push token.
  3. If the phone was unlocked or the session lock was not triggered (default 15 min for caregivers, CC-14), treat as possible exposure: check the audit log for views from that member after the loss time.
  4. Consider temporarily revoking the member (Care circle → remove) and re-inviting on a new device.
  5. Device data is encrypted with a non-extractable key (CC-26) — note in the assessment, but don't assume it ends the analysis.
  6. Severity: SEV-2 if views after loss; SEV-3 if none.

docs.title: 5.2 Suspicious access alert
docs.text:
Trigger: rules engine alert — a member opened 8+ parts of the record in 5 minutes or had 3+ denials in 10 minutes (CC-35).

  1. Guardian receives "Circle Care security notice" with in-app detail.
  2. Guardian confirms with the elder whether the access was expected.
  3. If not expected: remove the member's access, then contact support.
  4. Support reviews the audit log for that member; verify chain integrity.
  5. Assess whether the member is an account takeover (spoofing) or a legitimate member over-reaching (possible elder abuse concern — escalate per policy; see CC-8 Q12).

docs.title: 5.3 Leaked export file
docs.text:
1. Exports are passphrase-encrypted (PBKDF2-SHA256 250k → AES-256-GCM, CC-32). Determine whether the passphrase was also exposed.
  2. Identify the export event in the audit log (exported), who exported and when.
  3. If the passphrase was exposed or the file was weakly protected: SEV-2, breach assessment.
  4. Advise the circle; consider changing whatever the export revealed that can be changed (e.g., emergency contacts) — health history cannot be "rotated".

docs.title: 5.4 Vendor breach
docs.text:
1. Vendor notifies us (BAA terms in CC-30) or we learn from news.
  2. Determine what data the vendor held per the register. If the vendor was PHI-free by design (push, analytics), verify with logs that no PHI reached them.
  3. Rotate credentials/keys shared with the vendor.
  4. Obtain vendor's incident report, scope, timeline.
  5. Breach assessment for our notification duties.

docs.title: 5.5 SOS or escalation delivery failure
docs.text:
1. Switch to fallback channel (SMS fallback exists in the design, via: "sms-fallback").
  2. Notify affected guardians to check on elders directly.
  3. SEV-1 if platform-wide.

docs.title: 6. Breach notification — confirm with counsel
docs.text:
Which rule applies depends on CC-8 (business associate vs. consumer app). Timelines below are general understanding and must be confirmed with counsel for every incident.

Regime Who is notified Timeline (general understanding) HIPAA — as a business associate The covered entity (e.g., the agency) Without unreasonable delay, no later than 60 days from discovery; BAA may set shorter HIPAA — covered entity duties (the agency's) Individuals; HHS; media if more than 500 residents of a state or jurisdiction Individuals: no later than 60 days. HHS: within 60 days if 500+; annual log if fewer. Media: within 60 days if 500+ in a state FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (consumer mode) Individuals, FTC, media if 500+ residents of a state Confirm current timelines with counsel State breach laws Residents, sometimes attorneys general Vary by state; some shorter than 60 days

A HIPAA breach is presumed unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability of compromise (nature of data, who received it, whether it was actually viewed, mitigation). Document the assessment either way.

docs.title: 7. Communication templates (drafts)
docs.text:
To affected circle (guardian and elder):

Subject: Important information about your Circle Care account

On [date], we learned that [plain description]. The information involved may include [categories, no values]. We have [what we did]. You can [steps: review your access log, remove members, contact us]. We're sorry. Contact us at [contact] with any questions.

Plain language, large type, read-aloud friendly. Never include PHI in the notice email itself. Offer a phone call for elders.

To a partner agency (BA notice):

We are notifying you under our Business Associate Agreement of an incident discovered on [date] affecting [n] of your clients. Scope: [...]. Containment: [...]. We will provide a full report by [date].

Internal status update: time, severity, what we know, what we don't, actions, next update.

docs.title: 8. After the incident
docs.text:
• Post-incident review within 5 business days, blameless format.
  • Update this runbook, CC-10 threat model and CC-79 risk analysis.
  • Keep incident records at least 6 years (aligned with audit retention — confirm).

docs.title: RFP outline
docs.text:
1. Company background and product summary (link CC-10 threat model).
  2. Scope: environments, URLs, apps, API docs, test accounts per role (elder, guardian, family, pro, reviewer), out-of-scope items.
  3. Objectives: authorization bypass across circles and roles, pro@shift bypass, session/MFA weaknesses, PHI leakage via notifications/logs, document upload abuse, audit tampering, review console isolation.
  4. Rules of engagement: testing windows, no DoS on SOS paths without coordination, synthetic data only, emergency contact.
  5. Deliverables: executive summary, findings with CVSS and reproduction steps, ASVS/MASVS mapping, retest report.
  6. Vendor questions: team, credentials, sample report, insurance, BAA willingness, price, schedule.
  7. Evaluation criteria (§5) and timeline.

docs.title: pro@shift — minimum necessary for paid caregivers
docs.text: The matrix uses a special rule, pro@shift, for anything about the elder's health or daily care. A professional caregiver matches it only while checked in to a visit today (onShift()): visit.caregiverId === actor && visit.date === today && checkIn && !checkOut. When the shift ends, access to medicines, doses, tasks, notes and documents ends with it. Off shift, a caregiver still sees what they need to do their job safely: the circle (who to call), their schedule, the emergency card, SOS — and they can propose schedule changes and swaps.

docs.title: Sharing paused — ALWAYS_SHARED
docs.text:
When the elder turns on Pause sharing in the Privacy Center (settings.sharingPaused, CC-81), can() refuses every action by family and pro roles except on three resources:

const ALWAYS_SHARED: Resource[] = ["sos", "emergencyCard", "circle"];

So emergencies still work (SOS and the emergency card) and people still know who is in the circle. The guardian keeps access while sharing is paused because they hold legal authority; the public FAQ says the guardian "is told sharing is paused." The elder's own access is never affected.

docs.title: Refused actions are logged
docs.text: Most change actions in the store go through guard() in src/data/store.tsx (recordDose, verifyDose, saveMed, requestMedChange, decide, task actions, sosAcknowledge, saveShift, requestSwap, reviewDoc, invite, revoke, settings, exported — exceptions listed under Coverage gaps): if can() returns false, nothing changes and an audit entry with action "denied" is written. Three denials by one person within 10 minutes raise a security notice to the guardian (CC-35). Read access in the UI is checked with AccessGuard / useCan, which call the same can().

docs.title: Notable design choices to review
docs.text:
1. The elder cannot read guardian-only notes (notes.private read = guardian only). This conflicts with "the elder owns her data" and may conflict with a right of access where HIPAA applies (CC-8 Q13). Product decision needed.
  2. The elder can read but not write circle settings (settings write = guardian). The store makes an explicit exception: the elder may change her own fields in ELDER_SETTINGS (textSize, highContrast, readAloud, sharingPaused, elderLockMin, emergencyCard, toured) without the matrix check. Confirm whether she should also control things like her check-in window and quiet hours.
  3. Family can write doses, i.e., confirm a dose remotely. Consider requiring presence or limiting to "taken with me".
  4. Approvals are proposable by an off-shift pro ("pro" listed explicitly), unlike meds/tasks.

docs.title: Coverage gaps (prototype)
docs.text:
Closed on 2026-10-19. Every data-changing store action is now checked:

Action Check addNote, addDoc notes / notes.private write by visibility; docs / docs.legal write submitHandoff, acknowledgeHandoff new handoffs resource — write: pro@shift; read/ack: guardian, family, pro closeCircle data delete visitCheckIn professional caregivers only elderCheckin, elderAsk, elderSuggest the elder only sosResolve the elder (sos write) or a responder (sos respond) acceptShift the caregiver the shift was offered to acceptConsent the elder; or a verified guardian with a written reason

sosStart stays open so the presenter can trigger SOS in the demo; in production only the elder's device can raise it. All of these must still be enforced server-side.

docs.title: How it's tested
docs.text:
src/__tests__/policy.test.ts generates one test per cell: for every resource × action, it checks elder, guardian and family against the matrix, and checks the professional caregiver both on shift and off shift. It also checks:

  • unknown and revoked people get nothing;
  • pausing sharing limits family and caregivers to emergencies while the guardian keeps access;
  • only the review team can review legal documents.

Run npm test. On 2026-10-19 the full suite reported 180 tests passed across 4 files.

docs.title: Production enforcement (not built)
docs.text:
• The same MATRIX and can() must run in the API on every request (CC-19); the client copy is for UX only and can be bypassed.
  • On-shift status must come from server-recorded check-ins, not the device clock.
  • Reviewer access must be a separate internal app with its own authentication, MFA and audit.
  • Field-level filtering in responses (e.g., strip notes.private for non-guardians) rather than hiding in the UI.

docs.title: Writing guidelines
docs.text:
• Audience: someone who has never heard of Circle Care. Define terms or link to the Glossary.
  • Plain English, no hype. Short sentences. Active voice.
  • Be accurate to the code. Quote UI labels exactly, in bold for buttons and italics for on-screen text. Check thresholds and timings in the source. If the wiki and the code disagree, the code wins — fix the wiki.
  • Separate today from tomorrow. Use "In the prototype" for what the code does and "In production (planned)" for what is not built. Never describe the prototype as production-ready.
  • Fictional data only. Never add real names, health details or contact information.
  • Admonitions: !!! note, !!! info, !!! warning, !!! tip. Use note for privacy points.
  • Diagrams: fenced ```mermaid blocks.
  • Traceability: reference stories as CC-n, and update the Traceability matrix when a page gains or loses a story.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
• Save as .webp in docs/wiki/assets/screens/, named area-screen[-variant].webp (e.g. guardian-home-mobile.webp).
  • Use relative paths and the figure pattern with descriptive alt text, a caption and lazy loading:
<figure markdown="span">
  ![Describe what is on screen for someone who cannot see it](../assets/screens/guardian-home.webp){ loading=lazy }
  <figcaption>One sentence on why this screen matters.</figcaption>
</figure>
  • Add class="cc-phone" to the <figure> for phone-sized captures; wrap two figures in <div class="cc-pair" markdown> to show them side by side.
  • Use fictional demo data, reset the demo first, and mention anything unusual in the caption.

docs.title: Review process
docs.text:
1. Create a branch and make your change.
  2. Run mkdocs build --strict until it passes with no warnings.
  3. Open a pull request describing what changed and why; link the Notion story if there is one.
  4. Reviewers: the Product Owner (Sumanth) approves every change. Changes to security, privacy or compliance pages also need review by whoever owns that area (security officer / counsel once appointed).
  5. Check accuracy against the code, tone, screenshots and links.
  6. Merge; the maintainer publishes with mkdocs gh-deploy.
  7. Update Last updated on each feature page you changed and add a line to the Release notes if behaviour changed.

docs.title: Release 2 — Native & Connected
docs.text:
P4 · Jul 12 – Dec 31, 2027. Move from a web prototype to apps people can rely on: native notifications that wake a phone, real health data, real medicine data, and the languages Maggie's neighbours speak.

Epic Feature Value Native Mobile Apps iOS & Android apps with critical alerts SOS and missed high-priority doses break through silent mode — the one thing a web app cannot guarantee Watch companion & health sync Real heart rate, oxygen, activity and sleep through HealthKit / Health Connect, replacing simulated readings Health & Pharmacy Integrations FHIR medication import Medicine lists come from the prescriber's record instead of being typed in, reducing transcription errors Pharmacy refill integration Refill status and pickup appear on the calendar automatically Patient-portal appointment sync Doctor and lab appointments flow into the care calendar Language Access Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog app experience Serves the largest non-English-speaking older-adult and caregiver communities in California Translated notifications & care content Lock-screen text, reminders and instructions in each person's language

Success metrics (proposed targets): ≥ 95% of SOS alerts delivered to the first responder within 30 seconds · ≥ 90% doses confirmed in pilot circles · ≥ 60% of circles with at least one non-English user active weekly (where applicable) · app store rating ≥ 4.5.

docs.title: Release 3 — Insight & Safety
docs.text:
P5 · Jan 3 – Jun 25, 2028. Use the data the circle already shares to prevent problems: trends instead of single readings, safer medicines, falls and wandering, and scams.

Epic Feature Value Proactive Health Insights Trend alerts Flags gradual changes (e.g. resting heart rate rising over a week) before they become emergencies Weekly AI health summary A plain-language weekly summary for the guardian — descriptive, never diagnostic Doctor-visit report PDF One-page report of readings, adherence and notes to bring to appointments Medication Safety Refill tracker & low-supply alerts Nobody runs out of a critical medicine Photo pill check Caregiver or elder confirms the right pill by photo Drug-interaction check Warns when a new medicine may interact with current ones Wearables & Fall Detection Wearable fall detection Automatic SOS when a fall is detected and not cancelled Inactivity monitoring Gentle check when there is no movement at unusual times Safe zones & wandering alerts Guardian alerted if the elder leaves an agreed area at unusual hours — with the elder's consent Fraud & Scam Protection One-tap scam report & guardian alert Elder reports a suspicious call or message; guardian is told Scam-awareness coaching Short, respectful tips on current scams

Success metrics (proposed targets): median time from abnormal trend to guardian review < 24 hours · zero missed critical refills in pilot circles · fall-alert false-positive rate < 5% · ≥ 70% of elders keep safe-zone consent on after 30 days · reported scam attempts acted on within 1 hour.

docs.title: Release 4 — Connected Family
docs.text:
P6 · Jul 3 – Dec 22, 2028. Make daily life easier for everyone in the circle — not only safer.

Epic Feature Value Elder Independence & Connection Voice-first assistant Maggie asks "What's next?" or "Call Sarah" hands-free (on-device where possible) Memory aids Gentle prompts for names, places and routines One-tap video calls Faces, not just voices, with the people she chose Daily feeling, hydration & meal check-ins Richer, optional self-reported well-being Caregiver Support & Workforce Voice visit notes Caregivers dictate the hand-off instead of typing Photo proof of care Optional photos for tasks such as wound care or meals Caregiver burnout check-in Early warning for overloaded family and professional caregivers Shift marketplace Fill open shifts from trusted, vetted caregivers Timesheets & invoices Hours from verified visits become timesheets and invoices Guardian Admin & Finance Care expense & benefits tracker Tracks costs and benefits such as Medicare or long-term-care insurance Legal & insurance document vault with renewal reminders POA, insurance cards and directives in one place, with expiry reminders Guided care-plan builder Step-by-step care plan for new guardians Care Access Services Telehealth visits Video appointments from the calendar Ride booking for appointments Book transport for medical appointments Family group chat Conversation for the circle, with the same privacy rules

Success metrics (proposed targets): elder weekly active rate ≥ 80% · hand-off completion ≥ 95% of shifts · open-shift fill rate ≥ 90% within 48 hours · guardian-reported time on admin down 30% · caregiver burnout check-in response ≥ 50%.

docs.title: Release 5 — Agency & Growth
docs.text:
P7 · Jan 8 – Jun 30, 2029. A sustainable business: home care agencies as customers and a family subscription.

docs.title: Security & privacy
docs.text:
This page explains the security and privacy controls that are real code in the prototype, how they work, and what a production system still needs. Detailed working documents: threat model (CC-10), permission matrix (CC-18), security test plan (CC-78), incident response runbook (CC-34), HIPAA risk analysis (CC-79).

Prototype, not a compliant system

The prototype demonstrates privacy-by-design with fictional data in one browser. It has not been security-reviewed or penetration-tested, has no backend, and must not be used with real health information.

docs.title: Encryption at rest
docs.text:
src/lib/secureStorage.ts (CC-26, CC-27):

  1. On first use the app generates an AES-GCM 256-bit key with crypto.subtle.generateKey(…, extractable = false, ["encrypt", "decrypt"]) and stores the CryptoKey object in IndexedDB (circle-care-keys). Because it is non-extractable, no JavaScript — including the app's own — can read or export the raw key bytes.
  2. Every save serialises the state to JSON and encrypts it with a fresh random 12-byte IV. The result is stored as enc:v1:<base64 iv>:<base64 ciphertext> in localStorage["circle-care-demo"].
  3. Loading decrypts with the same key. GCM authentication means a modified ciphertext or a missing key fails closed: the app starts a fresh demo instead of reading tampered data.
  4. Documents are encrypted the same way in IndexedDB circle-care-files.
  5. If Web Crypto or IndexedDB is unavailable, the prototype falls back to plain localStorage (demo convenience only).

The e2e test CC-26 data at rest in the browser is encrypted checks that the stored value starts with enc:v1: and does not contain "Maggie".

Threat-model note

Browser-side encryption protects data from casual inspection of storage, backups and other origins. It does not protect against malicious code running in the page itself, which is why the CSP and a minimal dependency footprint matter.

docs.title: Tamper-evident audit log
docs.text:
src/data/audit.ts and src/lib/sha256.ts (CC-28):

hash(entry) = SHA-256( JSON.stringify([id, at, actorId, action, resource, prev]) )
prev(first) = "000…0" (64 zeros)
prev(n)     = hash(n − 1)
  • verifyChain() walks the log and reports the first entry whose prev or hash does not match — catching edits, deletions and reordering. The Privacy Center shows "Access log is intact — All N entries check out" or "Entry N of M doesn't match its seal."
  • Entries store identifiers and resource names only, never health values.
  • RETENTION_YEARS = 6 documents the intended retention.
  • SHA-256 is implemented in pure JavaScript so the chain can be computed synchronously; a unit test compares it with Node's crypto for edge-case inputs.

Limitation: an attacker who controls the device can rewrite the whole chain consistently. Production anchors the chain externally (e.g. periodic hashes to a separate write-once store).

docs.title: Privacy shield and session lock
docs.text:
• Privacy shield (PrivacyShield in Extras.tsx): when the page becomes hidden (visibilitychange, pagehide), a blank cover with the logo replaces the screen so the app-switcher snapshot shows no health data.
  • Session lock (AppShell): after sessionLockMin minutes without pointer, key, scroll or touch activity (default 15 for caregiver and guardian; elder off by default, 5 or 15 by choice) a lock screen covers the app: "We lock the app after 15 minutes without activity so others can't see Maggie's information."

docs.title: Export encryption
docs.text:
encryptWithPassphrase() (CC-32): passphrase → PBKDF2-SHA-256, 250,000 iterations, random 16-byte salt → AES-256-GCM key → encrypt with a random 12-byte IV. The .ccexport file is JSON:

{ "format": "circle-care-export", "v": 1, "kdf": "PBKDF2-SHA256-250000",
  "cipher": "AES-256-GCM", "salt": "…", "iv": "…", "data": "…" }

Passphrases must be at least 8 characters and are never stored; "We can't recover it for you." The e2e test checks that a downloaded file contains AES-256-GCM and does not contain Lisinopril.

docs.title: Deletion
docs.text: Close this circle (closeCircle, CC-33) requires data: delete (elder or guardian) and a typed DELETE. It removes the stored state, deletes the device key (making any remaining ciphertext unreadable), clears the encrypted file store, records a deletion timestamp, and reseeds the demo. Sign out everywhere (CC-27) signs every persona out and notifies the guardian.

docs.title: PHI-free notifications
docs.text: Every alert has a generic title (what the lock screen shows) and a separate detail shown only inside the unlocked app. Titles in use: You have a reminder from Circle Care, Circle Care needs your attention, Emergency alert from Circle Care, Circle Care security notice, Circle Care health notice, and similar. The weekly digest email shows only counts. See Alerts & notifications.

docs.title: Anomaly detection
docs.text: Signal Threshold Action Bulk record viewing ≥ 8 viewed entries by one non-elder actor within 5 minutes Guardian security notice Repeated refusals ≥ 3 denied entries by one actor within 10 minutes Guardian security notice

docs.title: HIPAA posture
docs.text:
Circle Care is designed to the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules. Whether HIPAA applies depends on the business model:

Model Likely regime Consumer app used directly by families FTC Health Breach Notification Rule and state health-privacy laws Sold to home care agencies or providers Circle Care is a business associate; HIPAA applies and BAAs are required

See the regulatory memo (CC-8) — not legal advice.

docs.title: What production needs
docs.text:
1. The same permission policy enforced in a server API, with field-level filtering of responses.
  2. Server-side encryption at rest with managed, rotated keys; TLS in transit.
  3. The audit chain stored server-side and anchored externally; 6-year retention.
  4. Signed BAAs with every vendor that touches health data (hosting, database, push/SMS/email, error monitoring) — vendor register.
  5. Real push/SMS delivery and iOS critical-alert entitlements.
  6. Identity and legal-document verification by a staffed review team in a separate internal app.
  7. Breach response — incident response runbook with assigned roles and a tabletop exercise.
  8. A third-party penetration test (OWASP ASVS L2 / MASVS) — security test plan.
  9. A designated security officer owning the risk analysis.
  10. HTTP security headers (frame-ancestors, HSTS) from the host.

docs.title: State model
docs.text:
• One state object (State in src/data/types.ts) holds the whole circle: members, medicines, doses, tasks, shifts, visits, hand-offs, SOS events, check-ins, approvals, notes, documents, appointments, health settings, audit log, alerts and settings. See Data model.
  • Updates go through update(fn): the state is deep-copied with structuredClone, the action mutates the draft, evaluate() runs, and React re-renders.
  • Actions (actions in useStoreState) are the only way to change data. Each guarded action calls guard(state, action, resource) → can(); refusals change nothing and write a denied audit entry.
  • Selectors (src/data/selectors.ts) compute derived views — dose states, next item, late check-ins, coverage gaps, streaks, adherence, North Star, activity feed.
  • Demo clock: clock(state) = now + clockOffsetMin so presenters can skip ahead.
  • Versioning: STATE_VERSION = 6. A stored state with another version is discarded and reseeded.
  • Persistence: saves are debounced by 250 ms and flushed on pagehide. See Security & privacy.
  • Read logging: logView(resource) writes a viewed entry at most once per resource every 10 minutes.

docs.title: Rules engine
docs.text:
evaluate(state) in src/data/store.tsx is a pure function over the state draft. It runs every 15 seconds (setInterval) and after every action.

Order Rule Story 1 Dose repeat reminder at +10 min; caregiver and guardian escalation at their thresholds CC-39, CC-42, CC-43 2 Missed check-in: elder prompt after window end; guardian at +15 min CC-52 3 Late caregiver check-in (> 15 min) CC-57 4 SOS escalation step every escalationDelayMin minutes CC-48 5 Approval waiting > 24 h CC-64 6 Suspicious access: ≥ 8 views in 5 min, ≥ 3 denials in 10 min CC-35 7 Unusual vital signs (if shared) CC-86, CC-88 8 Expire time-limited members CC-25

pushAlert() ignores an alert whose key already exists, which makes the engine idempotent. Full catalogue: Alerts & notifications.

In production (planned): the same rules run server-side on a scheduler, independent of any open browser, with delivery through a notification service.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A rules engine turns time and state into alerts: missed doses, missed check-ins, late caregivers, SOS escalation, stale approvals, suspicious access, unusual health readings and expired access. Each alert has a lock-screen title that never contains health information and an in-app detail shown only after the app is unlocked. Alerts appear as a banner when they arrive and in the Alerts list (bell icon).

Why. Families are buried in messages; health details on a lock screen are a privacy breach waiting to happen. Circle Care is "quiet unless it matters" — and when it speaks, the lock screen says only "You have a reminder from Circle Care."

Business value. Trustworthy, low-noise alerting is what lets the guardian stop calling every day, and PHI-free notification text is a prerequisite for using third-party push and SMS providers.

docs.title: User journey
docs.text:
1. Something happens (e.g. a dose passes its threshold). Within 15 seconds the rules engine creates an alert.
  2. If the recipient has the app open, a banner slides in: Circle Care · now · the lock-screen title, and "Lock-screen text above has no health details. Tap to see more." Critical alerts are red. Banners disappear after 7 seconds.
  3. Tapping the banner opens the relevant screen.
  4. The bell shows an unread count. Alerts lists each alert with its in-app detail, "Lock screen showed: "…"", and the age. Alerts are marked read 1.5 seconds after the list opens.
Every alert shows the generic lock-screen text it would have displayed.

docs.text: evaluate(state) in src/data/store.tsx runs every 15 seconds while the app is open and after every change. Alerts are de-duplicated by key, so a rule fires once per condition (per dose slot per day, per SOS step, per 10-minute window for security rules).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A full-month calendar of appointments that relate to Maggie's medicines: doctor visits, pharmacy refills, lab tests and medication reviews. Each appointment records who it is with, where, which medicines it concerns, who is taking Maggie, and how to prepare. An Up next banner keeps the next few appointments in view.

Why. Medication safety depends on more than doses: refills must be picked up, fasting lab tests must be prepared for, and follow-ups must have someone to drive. These usually live in one person's head or phone.

Business value. Reduces missed refills and appointments, and links each appointment to the medicines it concerns — the foundation for Release 2 patient-portal appointment sync and pharmacy refill integration.

Tapping it jumps to that day.

  4. Selecting a day fills the day panel: type, title, time range, provider and location, About: Metformin, Ana is taking her, preparation notes, and Edit, Done (today or earlier) and Cancel.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. The care circle is the set of people allowed to help Maggie, each with a role that decides what they can see and do. The guardian invites people by role, can make access temporary, and sets the SOS order. Maggie sees everyone and can remove anyone except her legal guardian. A guardian's legal powers depend on a power-of-attorney or guardianship document that an internal review team verifies.

Why. Shared family logins and group chats give everyone everything. Care requires the opposite: the right person sees the right thing, only for as long as needed, and the elder can see and change it.

Business value. Role-based, time-bound access is what makes Circle Care safe to recommend to agencies and acceptable to elders. Guardian verification protects against the most serious abuse risk: someone falsely claiming authority over an older adult.

  3. Who gets SOS alerts first lists the escalation order — "Sarah · immediately", "Ana · after 2 min without an answer", "James · after 4 min without an answer" — with up/down arrows. "Maggie can see this list in her emergency screen."
  4. Legal authority lists POA or guardianship documents with In review, Verified or Needs resubmission. In the demo, In review items have a Simulate approval button.
