docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. Sarah sets up recurring shifts and assigns caregivers, who accept them. Ana checks in at Maggie's door, which unlocks the care plan for the shift; the guardian sees who is with Maggie now. At the end of the shift Ana sends a hand-off — drafted automatically from what she logged — and the next caregiver reads and acknowledges it. Late arrivals and uncovered shifts are flagged to the guardian before they become problems.

Why. "Half my morning is figuring out what happened yesterday." (caregiver hypothesis, CC-3). Coverage problems are usually discovered too late, and verbal hand-offs lose information.

Business value. Verified visits are evidence of care for families and, later, agencies (electronic visit verification is a Release 5 item). The self-drafting hand-off removes the most-skipped paperwork from a caregiver's day.

docs.text: Feature ID / area F-02 · Elder app (/app/elder) Personas Maggie (elder) Status Built in prototype — voice depends on browser support for on-device speech recognition Related stories CC-39 reminder card · CC-40 taken / skipped / refused · CC-48 SOS-list suggestion · CC-52 daily check-in · CC-65 decisions visible to the elder · CC-68 three-action home · CC-69 call my person · CC-70 text size & contrast · CC-71 colour contrast · CC-72 read-aloud · CC-73 voice confirmation · CC-14 elder lock option Last updated 2026-10-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A deliberately small app for the older adult: one home screen with three large actions — What's next, SOS and Call my person — plus a morning "I'm OK" check-in, medicine reminders that can be read aloud or answered by voice, a list of decisions made about her care, and simple display settings.

Why. The landing page puts it plainly: "Designed for 81, not 21." Older adults abandon apps with menus, small text and jargon. Every elder screen shows one thing at a time, in large type, with buttons of at least 48 px.

Business value. The elder is the person whose adoption the whole circle depends on. A simple, respectful experience increases dose confirmation and daily check-ins (both inputs to the North Star) and reduces worried phone calls for the guardian.

docs.title: User journey
docs.text:
1. Maggie opens the app and sees today's date and a greeting — "Good morning, Maggie" (before noon), "Good afternoon" (until 5 PM), "Good evening".
  2. From one hour before the check-in window opens until she checks in, a banner asks "How are you this morning?" — "Let Sarah know you're OK." She taps I'm OK. Toast and spoken confirmation: "Sarah will see you're OK". The banner becomes "You checked in at 8:40 AM".
  3. The What's next tile shows the single most important item, e.g. "Up next · 6:00 PM — Metformin — 1 tablet. Take with food." A speaker button reads it aloud.
  4. She taps the tile to open the reminder card (see below) and answers I took it, Skip this time or I don't want to take it.
  5. The red SOS tile opens the hold-to-send screen (SOS & emergency).
  6. The green Call my person tile ("Sarah and 2 more") opens Who would you like to call? with large photo cards for up to three favourite people; each is a one-tap phone call.
  7. Below the tiles: Updates about me (a red dot when there is a new decision), My privacy, Emergency card and Text size.
Elder home: three actions and four small links. Reminder card with voice answer.

docs.title: Reminder card (CC-39, CC-40, CC-73)

1. The card shows a badge (Time to take it · time when due, Coming up · time otherwise), a drawing of the pill in its real colour and shape, name, strength and dose, instructions and "For your blood sugar. Prescribed by Dr. Hannah Brooks."
  2. I took it → "Great — marked as taken". Skip this time → "OK — marked as skipped".
  3. I don't want to take it → "That's your choice. Would you like to tell Sarah why? (optional)" with a free-text box ("For example: it upsets my stomach") → Send → "Got it. Sarah will see your note".
  4. Answer with my voice → "Listening… say "I took it" or "skip"". The answer is recorded the same way as a tap.
  5. Later today lists up to five upcoming doses and tasks.
  6. When the next item is a task (e.g. Drink a glass of water), the card shows a single Done button → "Nice work!".

  2. I have a question opens a text box → Send to Sarah. Sarah sees "Maggie has a question" at the top of Approvals.
Every decision about Maggie is visible to her.

  3. Lock Circle Care: Never lock (default), After 5 minutes, After 15 minutes — "If other people use your phone, Circle Care can lock itself when you're not using it."
  4. Who we call when you press SOS shows the numbered escalation list. Want a change? Tell Sarah. sends a suggestion ("For example: call Ruth before James").

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. The guardian's command centre. Home answers "Is Mom OK today?" in seconds and lists only the things that need Sarah. Approvals is where medicine changes, new members and shift swaps wait for her decision. Activity is the full history; the Weekly digest is the summary; Settings controls how and when she is alerted.

Why. "I find out about problems days later, from someone else." (guardian hypothesis, CC-4). Remote decision-makers need signal, not noise — and the elder must be able to see what was decided about her.

Business value. Reduces anxiety-driven calls and missed problems; makes the guardian's legal role concrete (approvals) while keeping the elder informed. The digest is the retention loop for family buyers.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A Health section for the guardian with three tabs. Summary highlights today's numbers and any unusual readings. Heart & oxygen charts heart rate and blood oxygen across the day against Maggie's usual range, with every unusual reading explained and a full readings table, plus 30-day weight. Activity shows daily goals, how each hour was spent, steps by hour, last night's sleep stages and a 7-day mood view. Readings arrive every 30 minutes from Maggie's watch — only while Maggie chooses to share them.

Why. Families worry about the hours between visits. A watch already collects useful signals, but raw data is overwhelming and sharing it without the elder's consent is a privacy failure.

Business value. Turns wearable data into a small number of plain-language signals, positions Circle Care for the Release 3 "Insight & Safety" epics, and demonstrates consent-driven sharing of sensitive data.

Not a medical device

Every Health page ends with: "Demo readings are simulated. In the full product they sync from Maggie's watch through Apple Health or Health Connect, only while she chooses to share them. Circle Care isn't a medical device; call 911 in an emergency." Alert thresholds are a guardian preference; the settings page advises "Ask Maggie's doctor what range is right for her."

docs.text:
1. Sarah taps Health (tab bar or side menu). The header reads "From Maggie's watch · new reading every 30 min · last 4:00 PM, next 4:30 PM" with an Alert settings link.
  2. Summary opens with an attention panel — "2 unusual readings today" (e.g. 3:00 AM Blood oxygen low: 89%; 2:30 PM Heart rate high: 128 bpm) and See trend — or "All readings in Maggie's usual range today".
  3. Highlights cards: Heart rate, Blood oxygen (each with a sparkline and today's range), Resting heart rate, Steps, Stand hours, Walking, Sleep last night, State of mind, Weight (30-day change) and Height · BMI. Cards open the relevant tab.
  4. Heart & oxygen shows a day stepper (Today, Yesterday, … up to 6 days back). The heart-rate chart shades the usual range (50–110 bpm) and marks unusual points; the oxygen chart draws an "Alert below 92%" line. Each chart lists its unusual readings with a tag (High, Low, Sudden change).
  5. Show all readings as a table reveals every reading with time, heart rate, oxygen and a note (Asleep or the flag).
  6. Activity shows three goal rings (stand hours, walking minutes, steps), How Maggie spent today so far (one coloured block per hour: sleeping, sitting or resting, standing, walking), Steps by hour, Sleep · night before with stage rows (Awake, REM, Core, Deep) and the 7-hour goal, and Mental well-being · 7 days from her check-in moods, with caregiver visits and mindful minutes.
  7. If Maggie turns sharing off, the page shows "Maggie isn't sharing health readings" — "She can turn this back on in her Privacy Center. Medicines, check-ins, the calendar and SOS work as usual."

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. The guardian maintains Maggie's medicines and daily routines. Each dose appears for Maggie as a reminder and for Ana as a checklist item. Every dose ends up taken, skipped or refused — with a name, a time and, when given during a shift, a caregiver-verified mark. Unconfirmed doses escalate: first to the caregiver, then to the guardian, twice as fast for high-priority medicines. Caregivers and family can request changes; only the guardian (or Maggie) changes the plan.

Why. Medication errors are the most common and most dangerous failure in home care. When three people share responsibility, the problem is usually not forgetfulness but not knowing what someone else already did.

Business value. Dose confirmation is the core of the North Star metric. Verified doses give families and agencies evidence of care; escalation reduces the time an unconfirmed dose goes unnoticed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. A shared notebook for the circle. Anyone allowed can post a note to Everyone or to Sarah only. Documents — care plans, discharge summaries, legal papers — are checked by their real file type, encrypted on the device, and opened in a viewer that watermarks the viewer's name and the time across the page. Every view goes into Maggie's access log.

Why. Care information arrives as scattered texts and paper. Some of it is sensitive (a family concern, a legal document) and should not be visible to everyone; documents copied out of an app are a common source of leaks.

Business value. One place for the circle's context; a defensible model for sensitive documents that agencies and compliance reviewers expect.

docs.title: User journey
docs.text:
1. Sarah (or Ana while on shift) opens Notes & documents — "Shared with the circle".
  2. She writes in "Share an update with the circle…", picks Everyone or Sarah only, and taps Post note ("Note posted"). The hint explains who will see it.
  3. Notes list shows author, time ("2 days ago") and visibility (Everyone or a lock and Sarah only).
  4. Documents lists each file with type, size, uploader and date, plus Verified, In review or Resubmit badges for legal documents, and View.
  5. To upload, she picks a type (Care plan, Discharge summary, Legal authority (guardian only), Other) and taps Upload. "PDF, PNG or JPEG up to 10 MB. Files are checked, encrypted on this device and shown with the viewer's name watermarked across them. In the full product they're also virus-scanned on our servers."
  6. A wrong file type is rejected: ""fake.pdf" isn't a PDF, PNG or JPEG file. Only those types can be uploaded." A valid file is added ("Document added", or "Sent for verification" for legal authority).
  7. View opens the document with a repeating watermark such as "Sarah · Oct 19, 2026, 4:08 PM". "Watermarked for Sarah · … This view was added to Maggie's access log."
Notes with per-note visibility, and encrypted documents.

What. A Join the pilot page recruits families for an 8-week pilot. Inside the app, a one-question Net Promoter Score survey collects feedback without health details. An internal pilot dashboard shows aggregate results and hides any group smaller than five. Demo mode lets a presenter switch persona and simulate events.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. One page where the elder sees and controls her information: pause sharing, choose whether her health readings are shared, see who can see her information and who looked at it, check that the access log is intact, download an encrypted copy, review what she agreed to, sign out everywhere, and close the circle. The guardian sees the same page in read-only form for the sharing switches.

Why. "Her data. Her decision." is Circle Care's core promise. Without a place to exercise it, privacy is only a policy.

Business value. The Privacy Center is the clearest differentiator from monitoring-style competitors (competitive teardown) and directly supports HIPAA-style rights of access, accounting of disclosures and deletion.

docs.title: User journey
docs.text:
1. Maggie taps My privacy on her home screen: Your information, your choice (Sarah sees Maggie's privacy).
  2. Pause sharing — "Stops sharing with family and caregivers. SOS still works." When on: "Sharing is paused. Only SOS alerts go out." (toast "Sharing paused").
  3. Share health readings with Sarah — "Heart rate, blood oxygen, activity and sleep from your watch. Only Sarah can see them."
  4. Who can see your information lists every member with relationship, what they can see (e.g. "Today's plan, only during their shifts"), Invited and Access ends labels, and Remove (not for Sarah).
  5. Who looked at your information — the last 30 days of other people's actions: "James viewed care notes · 20 hr ago", "Ana created a shift hand-off · Yesterday".
  6. Download my data and What I agreed to ("Version 1.0, Thu, Aug 20.").
  7. Access log is intact — "All 9 entries check out. Each entry is sealed to the one before it, so any change or deletion would show up here."
  8. Open a downloaded copy and Sign out everywhere.
  9. What Circle Care keeps — counts of medicines, dose records, notes, documents and access-log entries; "Everything is encrypted, and nothing is sold or used for ads."
  10. Close this circle and delete its data.
Maggie's Privacy Center (full page, phone). Sarah's view: status badges, no switches.

docs.title: SOS & emergency
docs.text: Feature ID / area F-03 · Emergency response Personas Maggie (raises SOS), Sarah, Ana and James (responders) Status Partially built — the full flow works in-app; real push/SMS delivery, location and 911 integration are not built Related stories CC-46 hold-to-send SOS · CC-47 call 911 · CC-48 escalation chain · CC-49 acknowledge & resolve · CC-50 critical alerts break through silent mode · CC-52 missed daily check-in · CC-53 emergency card Last updated 2026-10-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
What. Maggie presses and holds SOS. After a 10-second chance to cancel, the people on her escalation list are alerted one after another — Sarah first, then Ana after 2 minutes, then James after 4 — until someone taps "I'm on my way." Maggie sees who is coming. The responder closes the event with a note of what happened. An emergency card gives first responders her allergies, conditions, medicines and contacts, and a daily check-in catches the quieter emergencies.

Why. A single phone call to a single relative is a fragile safety net. Personal emergency buttons exist, but they rarely tell the elder who is coming, and they are disconnected from the family's daily plan.

Business value. SOS is the feature families cite first when deciding to adopt a care app. Fast, visible acknowledgement is a pilot success metric (median alert answered in under 10 minutes — see Pilot & feedback).

Not an emergency service

Every SOS screen says: "Circle Care alerts your family and caregivers. It is not a monitored emergency service — call 911 if you are in danger." A Call 911 button is always visible.

docs.title: Raising an SOS (elder)
docs.text:
1. Maggie taps the red SOS tile on her home screen.
  2. Press and hold for help — a large round button with a progress ring. "Hold for 2 seconds. Your family and Ana will be told where you are." A secondary Call 911 button sits below.
  3. When the ring completes, Sending for help in 10 counts down. If read-aloud is on she hears "Sending for help in 10 seconds. Tap cancel if you're OK."
  4. She can tap Cancel — I'm OK ("Cancelled. No one was alerted.") or Send now.
  5. At zero, Help is on the way — "We're telling your family now." Who we're telling lists each person: Alerted, In 2 min if no answer, In 4 min if no answer.
Hold-to-send prevents accidental alerts. 10 seconds to cancel. The escalation chain, as Maggie sees it.

docs.title: Responding (guardian, caregiver, family)
docs.text:
1. Every guardian and caregiver screen shows a red bar: Maggie pressed SOS at 4:08 PM · Respond. A critical banner also appears.
  2. The responder screen: Maggie needs help — "Pressed SOS at 4:08 PM · Just now", location "At home · 412 Elizabeth St, Noe Valley, San Francisco (demo address)", buttons I'm on my way, Call Maggie and Call 911, and the escalation list with Alerted / Next / Responding badges.
  3. Tapping I'm on my way stops escalation and notifies everyone: "Sarah is responding to Maggie's SOS."
  4. Maggie's screen switches to the responder's photo and "Sarah is coming" — "Stay where you are if you can. Sarah answered at 4:09 PM."
  5. The SOS is closed either by Maggie (I'm OK now, recorded as "Resolved by Maggie — Sarah arrived.") or by the responder, who must type What happened? (required to close) and tap Mark resolved.
  6. With no active SOS, the responder page shows No active SOS — "Maggie is OK. If she presses SOS, you'll get an alert that breaks through silent mode." — and a list of Past alerts with outcomes.
The responder view on a phone.

docs.title: Emergency card (CC-53)

docs.title: About the product
docs.text:
What is Circle Care, in one sentence?

A care-coordination app that keeps an older adult, their caregivers and their legal guardian on the same daily plan, with the older adult in charge of who sees what.

Is Circle Care a real, available product?

No. It is a concept product built by Sumanth as a Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) training assignment and portfolio piece. The working prototype demonstrates the experience; it is not offered to the public and must not be used with real health information.

Who is it for?

Older adults who live at home and want help without losing independence; the professional and family caregivers who support them; and the legal guardian or healthcare power of attorney who makes decisions with them. See Personas.

How is it different from a medication reminder app or a family group chat?

It combines the pieces that usually live in separate tools — medicine schedules, caregiver shifts, check-ins, emergencies and decisions — around one person, and gives that person real control: a Privacy Center, an access log, one-tap pause, and visibility of every decision. Caregivers see care details only during their shifts. The competitive teardown frames the positioning to be validated.

What is the North Star metric?

Verified care tasks completed on time per week. In the prototype that is doses recorded as taken within 60 minutes of their scheduled time, plus completed care tasks, over the last 7 days. It is shown on the guardian's home screen and weekly digest.

docs.title: About the prototype
docs.text:
Is any of the data real?

No. Maggie, Sarah, Ana, James and Ruth are fictional. Phone numbers use the reserved 555-01xx range. Health readings are generated by a formula. Nothing leaves your browser.

Where is the data stored?

In your browser's local storage, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key that the browser will not let any script read or export. Each browser has its own separate copy. See Security & privacy.

What is the MFA code?

482913 — for every sign-in and for the sign-up flow. You can also tap the code on screen to fill it in.

Do notifications actually get sent?

No. The prototype shows in-app banners and an Alerts list. Real push, SMS and email delivery is planned for production.

Does the app use my location, camera or microphone?

Location: no — check-in shows the flow but does not read GPS. Microphone: only if you tap Answer with my voice on a reminder and your browser can recognise speech on the device; if recognition would need a cloud service, the feature stays off. Camera: no.

Why are some photos blank?

Stock photos are loaded from Unsplash and need internet access. Without it, they show as soft placeholders or coloured circles.

Can I install it on my phone?

Yes. Open the deployed URL in Safari (iOS) or Chrome (Android) and choose Share → Add to Home Screen. It opens full-screen and works offline after the first visit.

How do I reset everything?

Demo · Name → Reset demo. To also destroy the encryption key and uploaded files, use Privacy Center → Close this circle and delete its data as Maggie or Sarah.

docs.title: Privacy and compliance
docs.text:
Is Circle Care HIPAA compliant?

The prototype is designed to the HIPAA Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules, but it is not a production system and has not been assessed. Whether HIPAA legally applies depends on the business model: a consumer app families use directly is usually covered by the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule and state privacy laws instead; selling to home care agencies would make Circle Care a business associate. See the regulatory memo and HIPAA risk analysis.

Who can see Maggie's medicines?

Maggie, Sarah (her verified guardian), family members in her circle, and professional caregivers only while checked in to a shift. When Maggie pauses sharing, family and caregivers lose access to everything except SOS, the emergency card and the circle list. See the permission matrix.

Why does the guardian keep access when Maggie pauses sharing?

A healthcare power of attorney carries legal authority. The guardian keeps access but is told sharing is paused. Health readings are the exception: Maggie can stop sharing those with Sarah separately.

Can Maggie remove her guardian from the circle?

Not in the app. The Privacy Center explains that Sarah's access can only be changed through the legal process. Maggie can remove anyone else.

Is Circle Care a medical device or an emergency service?

No. The Health page and SOS screens say so explicitly: "Circle Care isn't a medical device; call 911 in an emergency" and "It is not a monitored emergency service — call 911 if you are in danger."

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms used across the product, the code and this wiki. Code identifiers are shown in monospace where a term maps directly to the data model.

Term Meaning Access log The record of who viewed, created, changed, approved, exported or was refused what, and when (AuditEvent). Shown to the elder and guardian in the Privacy Center. Never stores health values. See Tamper-evident. Acknowledge (hand-off) The next caregiver tapping I've read this on the previous shift's hand-off. Unread hand-offs appear on the guardian's attention list. Acknowledge (SOS) A responder tapping I'm on my way. This stops escalation and tells the elder who is coming. Adherence Share of scheduled doses recorded as taken. Shown per day in the weekly digest. Alert An in-app notification (Alert) with a PHI-free title (what the lock screen would show) and an in-app detail. Has a severity: info, warning or critical. Approval A request that waits for the guardian's decision: a medicine change, a new member or a shift swap (Approval.kind). The elder sees every decision. BAA Business Associate Agreement — the HIPAA contract required with any vendor that handles protected health information for a covered entity. Tracked in the vendor register. Care circle The elder plus everyone helping them: guardian, family and professional caregivers. One circle per elder. Care task / routine A recurring non-medicine activity such as breakfast, a shower or a walk (CareTask), daily, weekdays or weekends, assigned to the caregiver on shift or to the elder. Check-in (daily) The elder's one-tap I'm OK each morning, optionally with a mood. Expected inside the check-in window (default 08:00–10:00). Check-in / check-out (visit) A professional caregiver confirming arrival and departure for a shift (Visit.checkIn / checkOut). Location is confirmed once at each, or a manual reason is recorded. Consent The elder's agreement to the plain-language privacy terms (version and time stored). A verified guardian can accept on her behalf with a written reason. Coverage gap A scheduled shift with no caregiver assigned or not yet accepted. Critical alert An alert that breaks through silent mode (SOS, missed high-priority doses) when Emergencies break through silent mode is on. In the prototype this is a setting only; delivery is not built. Demo mode The Demo · Name pill at the top of the app, which opens the persona switcher and presenter controls (CC-80). Escalation (dose) An unconfirmed dose alerts the caregiver after 30 minutes and the guardian after 60 minutes by default; high-priority medicines escalate twice as fast (15 and 30 minutes). Escalation chain (SOS) The ordered list of people alerted when the elder presses SOS (default Sarah → Ana → James). The next person is added every 2 minutes until someone acknowledges. Elder The older adult the circle is built around. In the demo, Maggie. Emergency card A first-responder summary (allergies, conditions, medicines, directives, contacts) that the elder approves. Guardian / legal guardian The person with legal authority to make health decisions with or for the elder — here, Sarah as healthcare POA. Gets guardian permissions only after the review team verifies their documents. Hand-off The end-of-shift summary a caregiver sends at check-out: mood, meals, concerns, notes and a summary (Handoff). The prototype drafts the summary automatically (CC-82). High-priority medicine A medicine flagged critical (Lisinopril in the demo). Missed doses escalate twice as fast and are marked critical. HIPAA The US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. Circle Care is designed to its Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules; whether it legally applies depends on the business model (see the regulatory memo). k-anonymity (minimum cohort) On the pilot dashboard, any group with fewer than 5 responses is hidden so no one can be singled out. Minimum necessary The HIPAA principle that each person sees only the information needed for their role. In Circle Care, caregivers see care details only during shifts. MFA Multi-factor authentication — the 6-digit code step after the password. Demo code 482913. North Star The single metric the product optimises: verified care tasks completed on time this week (doses taken within 60 minutes of schedule plus completed care tasks over the last 7 days). NPS Net Promoter Score: % of 9–10 scores minus % of 0–6 scores, from −100 to 100. Collected in-app (CC-76). On shift (pro@shift) A professional caregiver with a check-in today and no check-out. The permission matrix grants care-detail access only in this state. Pause sharing The elder's one switch that limits family and caregivers to SOS, the emergency card and the circle list (CC-81). The guardian keeps access. PHI Protected health information — health data that identifies a person. Circle Care keeps PHI out of notifications, emails, the audit log and pilot data. POA (healthcare power of attorney) A legal document naming someone to make health decisions for a person. Sarah's POA is the demo's legal-authority document. Presenter controls Buttons in demo mode that fast-forward time or simulate events (missed dose, late caregiver, SOS…). Privacy Center The elder's (and guardian's) page for who can see her information, the access log, sharing switches, export, sign-out everywhere and closing the circle. Privacy shield A blank cover that replaces the screen when the app goes to the background so the app-switcher snapshot shows no health data. PWA Progressive Web App — a website that can be installed to a phone's home screen and opened offline after the first visit. Respite caregiver A temporary caregiver who covers for the usual one. Ruth in the demo, with 14-day access. Review team Internal Trust & Safety staff who verify legal-authority documents (CC-24). Rules engine The evaluate() function in src/data/store.tsx that turns time and state into alerts (missed doses, check-ins, late caregivers, SOS steps, reminders, suspicious access, abnormal vitals, access expiry). Runs every 15 seconds and after every change. Session lock The app locks after inactivity: 15 minutes by default for caregiver and guardian; off by default for the elder, who can choose 5 or 15 minutes. Suspicious access 8 or more record views by one person within 5 minutes, or 3 or more refused actions within 10 minutes, which alert the guardian (CC-35). Tamper-evident Each access-log entry stores a SHA-256 hash of itself and of the previous entry, so editing, deleting or reordering any entry breaks the chain and is detected. Time-limited access A member's expiresOn date after which their access is revoked automatically (CC-25). Verified dose A dose recorded by a caregiver who was checked in at the time (DoseLog.verified). Vitals Heart rate and blood oxygen readings from the elder's watch — simulated in the prototype every 30 minutes. Weekly digest The guardian's weekly summary: adherence, visits, check-in streak, North Star, and anything worth knowing. The email version contains no PHI (CC-83).

docs.title: Personas
docs.text:
Circle Care is designed around one care circle: an older adult at the centre and the people who help them. The prototype ships with one fictional circle in San Francisco, California. Each persona below is a design persona — the goals and pains are hypotheses to be validated by the research plan (CC-1 to CC-5), not findings from real interviews.

All personas are fictional

Names, relationships, phone numbers (+1 (415) 555-01xx) and health details are invented for the demo. Any resemblance to real people is coincidental.

docs.title: Maggie Lee — the elder
docs.text:
Margaret "Maggie" Lee, 80. Widowed, lives alone in her own home in San Francisco. Takes four medicines (blood pressure, blood sugar, vitamin D, cholesterol). Wears a watch that could share heart rate and activity. Still makes her own decisions.

Goals Stay in her own home. Remember her medicines without feeling nagged. Be able to get help fast. Keep her dignity and privacy. Pains Small text and busy screens. Feeling watched. Daily "just checking" phone calls. Not knowing what her family decided about her care. Quote (hypothesis) "I don't want to be watched. I want to be able to ask for help." What she uses Elder home (What's next, SOS, Call my person), reminders with read-aloud and voice answers, daily "I'm OK", Updates about me, Privacy Center, Emergency card, text size and lock settings. Permissions summary Reads everything about herself except guardian-only notes and caregiver hand-offs. Records her own doses and tasks (the matrix also lets her edit medicines, though the elder app offers no screen for it). Owns her emergency card. Invites and removes members (not her guardian). Pauses sharing, controls health-reading sharing, exports and deletes data. Cannot change guardian settings such as alert timing.

docs.title: Sarah Lee — the legal guardian
docs.text:
Sarah Lee, Maggie's daughter, holds a healthcare power of attorney (verified by the review team). Lives about two hours away, works full-time.

Goals Know Maggie is OK without calling three times a day. Make the important decisions (medicine changes, who joins the circle). Fill gaps in the caregiver schedule before they happen. Pains Finds out about problems days later, from someone else. Too many messages, none of them structured. Responsible for decisions without the information to make them. Quote (hypothesis) "I find out about problems days later, from someone else." What she uses Guardian dashboard, approvals, activity, digest and settings, Health, Calendar, Medications, Shift schedule, Care circle, Notes & documents, Alerts, SOS responder. Permissions summary Reads everything, including guardian-only notes. Writes medicines, schedule, appointments and settings directly. Approves or declines requests. Invites and revokes members. Can edit the emergency card, but her changes wait for Maggie's approval before they count as approved. Sees health readings only while Maggie shares them. Keeps access when Maggie pauses sharing. Can accept the privacy agreement on Maggie's behalf only once verified and with a written reason.

docs.title: Ana Rivera — the professional caregiver
docs.text:
Ana Rivera, home care aide from an agency. Works Monday to Saturday, 8:00 AM–2:00 PM. Uses her own phone, sometimes a shared one.

Goals Walk in and know exactly what this shift needs. Prove what she did. Hand off cleanly without writing an essay. Pains "Half my morning is figuring out what happened yesterday." Paper logs. Being blamed for missed doses she never knew about. What she uses Caregiver Today (check-in, doses, tasks), the end-of-shift hand-off, Schedule, Notes (on shift only), Emergency card, Alerts, SOS responder. Permissions summary Minimum necessary. Off shift she sees only the circle, the schedule, hand-offs, the emergency card, appointments and SOS. While checked in she can read medicines, doses, tasks, notes and documents, record doses and tasks, write hand-offs and guardian-only notes, and propose medicine changes. She can never approve, export, delete or see the digest or access log.

docs.title: James Lee — family member
docs.text:
James Lee, Maggie's grandson. Covers Sunday 10:00 AM–4:00 PM and is third in the SOS chain.

Goals Help on weekends without being the one in charge. Know what happened during the week. Pains Doesn't know what changed since last Sunday. What he uses (in the circle) Appears in hand-offs, SOS escalation, shift-swap targets and approvals (he requested Ruth's respite access). No dedicated sign-in view in the demo. Permissions summary Reads today's medicines, doses, tasks, notes, documents, history and appointments. Records doses and tasks, proposes medicine and schedule changes, responds to SOS. Loses everything except SOS, emergency card and circle when Maggie pauses sharing.

docs.title: Ruth Okafor — respite caregiver (time-limited)
docs.text: Ruth is invited to cover Ana's vacation. Her access is pending (she hasn't accepted yet and Sarah hasn't approved the request) and is set to end automatically after 14 days. She illustrates time-bound access (CC-25) and the invitation flow (CC-17).

docs.title: Review team — internal
docs.text: An internal Trust & Safety reviewer verifies legal-authority documents (power of attorney, guardianship orders). They see only the legal-document queue, nothing else about the elder (CC-24).
